extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of federal funding (K-12 school districts and institutions of higher education), Title IX Coordinators, campus administrators, and legal counsel responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and implementation guidance on what supportive measures are, when and to whom they must be offered, who must offer/coordinate them, limits on those measures, and illustrative examples under the final Title IX regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator duty to offer and coordinate supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(1)(ii) requires a Title IX Coordinator to offer and coordinate supportive measures under §106.44(g), as appropriate, for a complainant upon being notified of conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination and to offer and coordinate supportive measures for a respondent if the recipient has initiated grievance procedures under §106.45 (or §106.46) or has offered the respondent an informal resolution process under §106.44(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipient must require its Title IX Coordinator to offer and coordinate supportive measures; the Title IX Coordinator retains ultimate oversight but may designate designees or delegate duties to other staff best positioned to perform them. The Department will hold the recipient responsible for meeting obligations assigned to the Title IX Coordinator. (§§106.44(f)(1)(ii), 106.8(a))

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification obligations when complainant unknown or when complaint filed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a complainant is unknown, the Title IX Coordinator must notify the individual who reported conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination of the grievance procedures under §106.45 and the informal resolution process under §106.44(k), if available and appropriate. The Title IX Coordinator must notify a respondent of grievance procedures under §106.45 and the informal resolution process under §106.44(k), if available and appropriate, if a complaint is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification duties are required even when a complainant is unknown; notifications must include availability of grievance procedures and informal resolution options. (§106.44(f)(1)(iii)(A)-(B))

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'supportive measures' (§106.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are individualized measures offered as appropriate, as reasonably available, without unreasonably burdening a complainant or respondent, not for punitive or disciplinary reasons, and intended to restore or preserve equal access to education, protect safety, or provide support during grievance procedures or informal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final definition removes the words 'temporary' and 'deter the respondent from engaging in sex-based harassment,' clarifies that 'party' means 'complainant or respondent,' and aligns the definition's language with §106.44(g)(2) that measures must not be imposed 'for punitive or disciplinary reasons.' Supportive measures are permissive (recipient not required to provide every measure) and may impose burdens on the other party so long as not unreasonable. (See discussion of changes to §106.2 and §106.44(g)(2))

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on supportive measures (not for punitive/disciplinary reasons; not unreasonably burdensome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures may not be imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons and must not unreasonably burden a complainant or a respondent; they are subject to the limits in §106.44(g)(2) and may be challenged under §106.44(g)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although certain actions (e.g., no-contact orders) may also appear as disciplinary sanctions in a code of conduct, when used as supportive measures they cannot be imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons. Whether a measure is an 'unreasonable burden' is a fact-specific analysis. Departments clarified language to ensure measures protect safety of parties/educational environment and avoid bias against respondents. (§106.44(g)(2), (g)(4))

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification, termination, and challenge process for supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 106.44(g)(3) and (g)(4) permit a recipient to modify or terminate supportive measures as appropriate and provide parties the ability to seek modification or termination when a supportive measure does not meet the definition or when circumstances change materially (e.g., finding of non-responsibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may request modification/termination and recipients should allow review when measures no longer meet the definition or facts have materially changed. Supportive measures may be challenged under the procedures described in the regulations. (§106.44(g)(3)-(4))

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient responsibility and ability to delegate
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must offer and coordinate supportive measures, as appropriate; the Title IX Coordinator has ultimate oversight but the recipient may designate more than one employee to serve as Title IX Coordinator and may delegate specific duties to designees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation enables assignment of duties to personnel best positioned to perform them, addresses conflicts of interest, and aligns with administrative structures. However, the recipient remains ultimately responsible and must comply even if a state or local law would otherwise direct different arrangements. (§§106.44(g), 106.8(a), 106.6(b))

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and availability of supportive measures (regardless of formal complaint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures must be offered to complainants, as appropriate, regardless of whether grievance procedures are initiated, including when a complainant elects informal resolution or elects not to initiate grievance procedures. Supportive measures may be offered to respondents as appropriate, but the Title IX Coordinator must offer them only if grievance procedures have been initiated or an informal resolution process has been offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a recipient dismisses a complaint (e.g., because respondent cannot be identified), the recipient must still, as appropriate, offer supportive measures to the complainant (such as counseling). (§§106.44(f)(1)(ii), 106.45(d)(4)(i))

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of supportive measures (all forms of sex discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are available for all forms of sex discrimination, not limited to sex-based harassment, because Title IX obligations extend to ensuring access to education is not limited by any sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are designed to restore or preserve a party's access to the recipient's education program or activity, and need for support is not limited to harassment scenarios. (§106.44(a), §106.2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and risk analysis / consideration of community safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may consider the safety of the recipient's educational environment and the broader campus community when conducting a safety and risk analysis and in determining appropriate supportive measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(h) allows taking into account campus safety in safety/risk analyses; supportive measures may be designed to protect both parties and the educational environment. The Department permits consideration of community safety but declined to require offering measures to every community member engaged in grievance procedures. (§106.44(g), §106.44(h))

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and accessibility of information about supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to require recipients to publish additional information about supportive measures, to provide such information in particular formats or languages, or to require coordination with Principal Designated School Officials; recipients may, but are not required to, publish or otherwise make information available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain flexibility in how they meet the requirement to offer and coordinate supportive measures; nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from publishing additional information or providing translations so long as it complies with other regulations. (§106.44(g); §106.8(c)(1))

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative types/examples of supportive measures (§106.44(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides a non-exhaustive list of illustrative supportive measures (e.g., resubmission of an assignment, retake an exam, grade or transcript adjustments, tuition reimbursement or credit, medical/psychological services, advocacy, changes to transportation, housing relocation, emergency housing, assistance breaking leases, assistance with moving expenses, removal from participation on teams, trauma-informed care, counseling, support groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department retained an illustrative list to assist recipients while preserving discretion; it also clarified that supportive measures may include retroactive measures (e.g., retroactive withdrawals, extensions, transcript adjustments, tuition reimbursements) if reasonably available and appropriate to restore/preserve access. The list is illustrative, not exhaustive, and measures must be 'reasonably available.' (§106.44(g)(1))

rubrics_metrics.name: No-contact orders: permitted forms and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised language to allow 'restrictions on contact applied to one or more parties,' clarifying that recipients may impose mutual or non-mutual no-contact orders as supportive measures, subject to the rule that such orders must not be punitive or unreasonably burden a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In considering a no-contact order, a recipient should examine factors such as the need expressed by the party, ages of parties, nature of allegations and their ongoing effects, whether parties continue to interact (shared work, residence, classes), and whether mitigations (e.g., civil protective orders) exist. The Department rejected the assertion that no-contact orders are categorically a 'prior restraint' on speech and explained constitutional limits (Madsen v. Women's Health Ctr.). (§106.44(g)(1)-(2))

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability standard: 'reasonably available'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulation replaces the proposed phrase 'available and reasonable' with the standard 'reasonably available' to describe the expectation that supportive measures be provided when they are reasonably available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that a recipient is required to provide a supportive measure only where that measure is reasonably available given resources and circumstances; it addresses commenter confusion about prior phrasing. (§106.44(g)(1))

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary changes may be supportive measures (subject to burden analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'voluntary or involuntary' were removed from the final rule, and supportive measures may include involuntary changes in class, work, housing, or extracurricular assignments provided they are not imposed for punitive reasons and do not constitute an unreasonable burden on a complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an involuntary change is an unreasonable burden is fact-specific and depends on the particular circumstances of the party; the Department declined to categorically prohibit involuntary changes. (§106.44(g)(1))

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary burdensome supportive measures (§106.44(g)(2)): conditions and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures that impose burdens on a respondent may be permitted when necessary to protect a complainant's safety or access to education, so long as they are not punitive or disciplinary and do not unreasonably burden the respondent (or complainant). Final language emphasizes measures must not unreasonably burden a complainant or respondent and must be designed to protect the safety of the parties or the educational environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised concerns that burdensome measures could function as interim punishment without due process; the Department clarified limits and retained the recipient's discretion with the requirement that measures be non-punitive and not unreasonably burdensome. The regulations permit emergency removal under §106.44(h) for immediate threats, which is a separate provision. (§106.44(g)(2), (h))

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of confidential employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential employees (e.g., counselors, campus advocates) may provide direct supportive services but the Department declines to require them to be responsible for offering and coordinating supportive measures because confidentiality obligations may prevent necessary coordination across offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidential employees should explain how to contact the Title IX Coordinator when informed of conduct that may constitute sex discrimination; the Title IX Coordinator may then offer/coordinate supportive measures or initiate grievance or informal resolution processes. State laws that allow confidential employees different roles do not relieve the recipient of Title IX obligations. (§106.44(d)(2)(ii)-(iii); discussion of §106.44(g))

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy of records related to supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters expressed privacy concerns about records kept by Title IX Coordinators concerning supportive measures; the Department references §106.44(g)(5) and §106.44(j) for the discussion of privacy and recordkeeping limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should consult the provisions governing recordkeeping and privacy when maintaining records of supportive measures; the final regulations address privacy concerns but recipients remain responsible for Title IX compliance. (See discussion referencing §106.44(g)(5) and (j))
